sn35.92:2.2: The same “duality” is described as the (sentient) body and “external” name and form, which are essential for contact through the six senses ([sn12.19:1.3]()). One person who denied this duality is Yājñavalkya. This was, in fact, his culminating philosophy: “For when there is a duality, as it were, then one sees the other; one smells, tastes, hears, greets, thinks of, touches, and cognizes the other. But when this All has become the Self, how and what would one see? How and what would one smell, taste, greet, hear, think, touch, or cognize? By what would one cognize that which cognizes this All? This Self is not that, not that! … By what would one cognize the cognizer?” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14 = 4.5.15; readings vary). | This raises the question, how are we to reconcile this duality with the “duality” of existence and nonexistence, i.e. eternalism and annihilationsim ([sn22.90:9.2]()). Notice that the text does not say there can be no other duality; it says there can be no other duality for one who denies this duality. In other words, all dualities depend on this one. Now, Yājñavalkya denies this duality, yet asserts the truth of eternalism. The implication is that such an assertion is incoherent, for to make such an assertion relies on the duality of speech and the senses. For all his “nondual” talk, Yājñavalkya ends up asserting one axis of duality, namely the eternal survival of the soul.
